title: Set Operations: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
description: Combine result sets from multiple queries. Learn when to use UNION (concatenation), INTERSECT (overlap), and EXCEPT (difference).

data.text: Sometimes a single SELECT from one table isn't enough. You might need to append rows from two queries, find what they have in common, or find what one has that the other doesn't. SQL Server provides three set-based operators for exactly these scenarios.
UNION (or UNION ALL) appends the rows of one query below the rows of another. Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types.

data.title: UNION vs UNION ALL
data.code:
-- UNION removes duplicate rows
SELECT category_name FROM production.categories_2018
UNION
SELECT category_name FROM production.categories_2019;

-- UNION ALL keeps duplicates (faster)
SELECT category_name FROM production.categories_2018
UNION ALL
SELECT category_name FROM production.categories_2019;

data.title: UNION ALL is faster
data.text: UNION ALL is almost always faster than UNION because SQL Server does not need to sort and de-duplicate the combined result. If you know your two result sets cannot overlap, always use UNION ALL.
INTERSECT — rows in both result sets
INTERSECT returns only rows that appear in BOTH queries. It is the SQL equivalent of finding common ground.

data.title: Find categories that appear in both years

data.text: EXCEPT — rows in the first, not in the second
EXCEPT (also called MINUS in some databases) returns rows from the first query that do NOT appear in the second query. The order of operands matters.

data.title: Find categories from 2018 that did not continue to 2019

items: Both queries must return the same number of columns
Corresponding columns must have compatible data types
Column names come from the first (top) query
NULL values are considered equal to NULL in set operations
Set operators can be chained: a UNION b UNION c is evaluated left-to-right

data.title: Parentheses matter when chaining
data.text: When you mix UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT in one statement, SQL Server evaluates them left-to-right unless you add parentheses. Use parentheses to make your intent unambiguous.

data.title: Set operations cheat sheet
points: UNION combines rows and removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps duplicates (faster)
INTERSECT returns rows common to both queries
EXCEPT returns rows from the first query that are NOT in the second
All three require matching column counts and compatible types
Column names come from the first query; NULLs are equal across the two sides
